subject: Python for Interviews
summary: Interviewers form an opinion of your Python within the first ten lines you type. Not because they are counting idioms, but because fluent Python is a proxy for hours spent actually writing it: the candidate who reaches for Counter, unpacks tuples, and builds strings with join reads as someone who has shipped code, while the candidate who writes Java-in-Python — index loops, string += in a loop, manual counting dicts — reads as someone reciting a textbook. This subject is the working vocabulary: the three collections that solve most interview bookkeeping (Counter, defaultdict, deque), the sorting idioms built on key functions and stability, slicing, enumerate/zip/unpacking, heapq and bisect patterns that turn 20-line solutions into 5, and generators for the space-complexity conversation. It closes with the gotchas that actively lose offers — mutable default arguments, late-binding closures, is versus ==, shallow copies, the [[0]*n]*m trap — because knowing WHY they bite is the difference between a candidate who memorized rules and one who understands the object model. Every section's code runs and asserts its own claims, so you can paste any block and interrogate it.

sections.title: 1. Counter, defaultdict, deque: The Three Collections You Reach For
sections.content:
Most interview problems contain a bookkeeping sub-problem — count things, group things, or process things in order — and Python ships a purpose-built tool for each. Reaching for the right one matters twice: it shortens your code, and it tells the interviewer you know the standard library instead of re-deriving it under pressure.

Counter is a dict subclass for counting hashable things. Feed it any iterable and it produces value → count. The two behaviors that make it interview gold: a missing key returns 0 instead of raising KeyError (so no defensive `if k in d` dance), and most_common(k) gives you the top-k without writing a sort. Because two Counters compare equal when their counts match, `Counter(s) == Counter(t)` is a complete anagram check — one line, O(n), and it says exactly what it means.

defaultdict takes a factory function and calls it whenever you touch a missing key. defaultdict(list) is THE grouping idiom: `groups[key].append(item)` with no existence check, because the first touch creates the empty list. Use defaultdict(int) when you need counts you will keep mutating arithmetically; use Counter when you want counting-specific tools (most_common, +/- between counters).

deque (double-ended queue, pronounced 'deck') gives O(1) append and pop at BOTH ends, where a list's pop(0) / insert(0, x) are O(n) because every remaining element shifts left or right. The moment your solution says 'queue' — BFS is the classic — the idiomatic move is deque with append and popleft. Writing BFS with list.pop(0) is a known interview tell: the code works, but its hidden O(n) per dequeue makes the whole traversal quadratic, and a good interviewer will ask you why. Bonus tool: deque(maxlen=k) silently evicts from the far end as you append, giving you a self-maintaining last-k-items window for streaming problems.
sections.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque

# Counter: counting in one line; missing keys read as 0
votes = ["asha", "vik", "asha", "meera", "asha", "vik"]
c = Counter(votes)
assert c["asha"] == 3 and c["dev"] == 0          # no KeyError
assert c.most_common(1) == [("asha", 3)]

# Counter equality: complete anagram check
assert Counter("listen") == Counter("silent")

# defaultdict(list): the grouping idiom (group words by sorted letters)
words = ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]
groups = defaultdict(list)
for w in words:
    groups["".join(sorted(w))].append(w)   # first touch creates []
assert sorted(groups["aet"]) == ["ate", "eat", "tea"]

# deque: O(1) at both ends -> the BFS queue
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.appendleft(0)
assert q.popleft() == 0 and q.pop() == 3

# deque(maxlen=k): self-maintaining last-k window
last3 = deque(maxlen=3)
for x in range(10):
    last3.append(x)                        # old items fall off the left
assert list(last3) == [7, 8, 9]
print("collections idioms OK")

sections.title: 2. Sorting Idioms: key=, Stability, and itemgetter
sections.content:
Python's sort has one core design decision that unlocks every idiom: you never write a comparator (compare a to b); you write a KEY function that maps each element to a value, and elements are ordered by their keys. This is both faster — the key is computed once per element, not once per comparison — and more composable, because keys can be tuples.

Tuple keys are the multi-criteria idiom. `key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0])` means 'sort by field 1, break ties by field 0', because tuples compare element by element. For mixed directions on numeric fields, negate: `key=lambda s: (-s[1], s[0])` sorts score descending, name ascending, in one pass. When the key is a plain field lookup, `operator.itemgetter(1)` (or attrgetter('age') for objects) says the same thing with less lambda noise and runs measurably faster — mentioning it in an interview is a cheap fluency signal.

The second superpower is stability: Python's sort (Timsort) guarantees that elements comparing equal keep their original relative order. Stability is why the multi-pass idiom works: to sort by score descending then subject ascending, you may sort by the SECONDARY key first, then by the primary — the second sort preserves the first sort's order within each tie group. This matters when the directions cannot be expressed in one tuple key (for example, descending strings, which you cannot negate). It is also why 'is your sort stable?' is a real interview question with real consequences: an unstable sort would scramble ties and break this pattern.

Vocabulary check, because interviewers listen for it: `sorted(xs)` returns a NEW list and accepts any iterable; `xs.sort()` sorts a list in place, returns None (assigning its result is a classic bug), and is slightly cheaper. Both take key= and reverse=. Complexity for either: O(n log n) comparisons, O(n) extra space.
sections.code:
from operator import itemgetter

people = [("asha", 25), ("vik", 22), ("meera", 25), ("dev", 22)]

# key= maps each element to its sort key; ties keep input order (stable)
by_age = sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1])
assert by_age == [("vik", 22), ("dev", 22), ("asha", 25), ("meera", 25)]

# itemgetter: same result, clearer and faster for plain field keys
assert sorted(people, key=itemgetter(1)) == by_age

# tuple key: age ascending, then name ascending for ties
assert sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0]))[0] == ("dev", 22)

# mixed directions: negate the numeric field
scores = [("a", 3), ("b", 5), ("c", 3)]
best_first = sorted(scores, key=lambda s: (-s[1], s[0]))
assert best_first == [("b", 5), ("a", 3), ("c", 3)]

# stability exploited: sort by SECONDARY key first, then primary
rows = [("math", 90), ("bio", 90), ("math", 70)]
rows.sort(key=itemgetter(0))                 # secondary: subject asc
rows.sort(key=itemgetter(1), reverse=True)   # primary: score desc
assert rows == [("bio", 90), ("math", 90), ("math", 70)]

# .sort() returns None -- a classic bug when assigned
xs = [3, 1, 2]
assert xs.sort() is None and xs == [1, 2, 3]
print("sorting idioms OK")

sections.title: 3. Comprehensions vs Loops: When Each Wins
sections.content:
A list comprehension is a declarative sentence: 'the list of f(x) for every x in xs that passes this test.' When your intent IS map-and-filter, the comprehension states it in one line the interviewer can absorb at a glance, and it runs faster than the equivalent append loop because the loop machinery is executed in C rather than bytecode-by-bytecode. Dict and set comprehensions extend the same shape: `{w: len(w) for w in words}` and `{n % 3 for n in nums}` build lookups and deduplicated sets in place.

Know the grammar distinction interviewers probe: the trailing `if` FILTERS (element skipped entirely), while a conditional expression before the `for` TRANSFORMS every element ('pos' if n > 0 else 'nonpos'). They answer different questions and can combine in one comprehension.

Now the judgment half, because over-using comprehensions is its own tell. Reach for a plain loop when: (1) You need early exit — a comprehension always processes the whole iterable; a for loop can return or break the moment the answer is found. The hybrid idiom `next((x for x in xs if pred(x)), default)` gets lazy search in one line. (2) The body has side effects — appending to another structure, printing, writing I/O. `[out.append(n) for n in nums]` builds and throws away a list of Nones to smuggle in a side effect; every reviewer reads it as a smell, and interviews are reviews. (3) Nesting passes two levels or the logic needs intermediate names — a 120-character triple-nested comprehension proves cleverness and costs readability points; unroll it. (4) You need to accumulate ACROSS iterations (running max, state machines) — comprehensions map elements independently; carrying state belongs in a loop or functools.reduce.

The one-line rule of thumb to say out loud: 'comprehension when I am describing WHAT the collection is; loop when I am describing HOW a process unfolds.' Saying it while choosing is exactly the kind of reasoning interviews are designed to surface.
sections.code:
nums = [3, -1, 4, -1, 5, -9, 2]

# map + filter in one declarative line
squares_of_pos = [n * n for n in nums if n > 0]
assert squares_of_pos == [9, 16, 25, 4]

# dict and set comprehensions
name_len = {w: len(w) for w in ("tea", "chai", "espresso")}
assert name_len["espresso"] == 8
assert {n % 3 for n in (3, 6, 7, 10)} == {0, 1}

# conditional EXPRESSION transforms; trailing if FILTERS
labels = ["pos" if n > 0 else "nonpos" for n in nums]
assert labels.count("pos") == 4

# early exit: loop (or next() on a generator) beats a comprehension
def first_negative(xs):
    for x in xs:
        if x < 0:
            return x       # stops immediately
    return None
assert first_negative(nums) == -1
assert next((x for x in nums if x < 0), None) == -1

# side effects: use a loop; a comprehension would build a list of Nones
out = []
for n in nums:
    out.append(n * 2)
assert out[0] == 6 and len(out) == len(nums)

# carrying state across iterations belongs in a loop
running_max, best = [], None
for n in nums:
    best = n if best is None else max(best, n)
    running_max.append(best)
assert running_max == [3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5]
print("comprehension idioms OK")

sections.title: 4. Slicing Mastery: s[a:b:c] and Everything It Buys You
sections.content:
Slicing is Python's sub-sequence syntax: `s[start:stop:step]`, where stop is EXCLUSIVE and any part may be omitted. Negative indices count from the end (s[-1] is the last element), and a negative step walks backward — which is where `s[::-1]`, the reverse idiom, comes from. Half-open intervals are a design choice worth saying out loud in interviews: `s[:k]` and `s[k:]` partition the sequence with no overlap and no off-by-one, and `len(s[a:b])` is b − a. Two forgiving behaviors distinguish slicing from indexing: out-of-range slice bounds CLAMP instead of raising (s[5:100] quietly stops at the end, while s[100] raises IndexError), and a slice of a list always returns a NEW list — Python has no cheap 'view' of a list the way NumPy arrays or Go slices share memory. That copy semantics cuts both ways. It gives you the copy idiom `a[:]` (equivalent to list(a) and a.copy()): essential when you need to mutate a copy while keeping the original, or iterate over a snapshot while modifying the source. But it also means every slice costs O(k) time and memory for k elements — recursing on `xs[1:]` at every level, a pattern copied from functional languages, silently turns a linear algorithm quadratic; pass indices instead. Interviewers who see slicing in your recursion WILL ask about its cost.

Lists add slice ASSIGNMENT: `xs[1:3] = [9]` splices a replacement in place (lengths need not match), and `del xs[:2]` drops a range. These mutate the original — the reason `xs[:] = new_values` rebinds contents while every alias to xs sees the change.

Idioms to have at your fingertips: reverse with s[::-1]; palindrome check `s == s[::-1]`; every-second element s[::2]; rotate right by k as `xs[-k:] + xs[:-k]` with k reduced modulo len(xs) first — the modulo guards both k = 0 and k larger than the length, and interviewers deliberately test those edges.
sections.code:
s = "interview"

# start:stop(exclusive):step; negatives count from the end
assert s[0:5] == "inter" and s[-4:] == "view"
assert s[::2] == "itriw"
assert len(s[2:7]) == 7 - 2

# reverse and the palindrome one-liner
assert s[::-1] == "weivretni"
assert "racecar" == "racecar"[::-1]

# slices clamp out-of-range bounds; indexing raises
assert s[5:100] == "view"
try:
    s[100]
    raised = False
except IndexError:
    raised = True
assert raised

# a slice of a list is a NEW list: copy vs alias
a = [1, 2, 3]
alias, snapshot = a, a[:]
a.append(4)
assert alias == [1, 2, 3, 4] and snapshot == [1, 2, 3]

# slice assignment and deletion mutate in place
xs = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
xs[1:3] = [9]                  # lengths need not match
assert xs == [0, 9, 3, 4]
del xs[:2]
assert xs == [3, 4]

# rotate right by k, edge-safe via modulo
def rotate(xs, k):
    k %= len(xs)
    return xs[-k:] + xs[:-k] if k else xs[:]
assert rotate([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2) == [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]
assert rotate([1, 2, 3], 3) == [1, 2, 3]      # k == len -> unchanged
print("slicing idioms OK")

sections.title: 5. enumerate, zip, and Unpacking: Iteration Without Index Arithmetic
sections.content:
The fastest way to look like a C programmer writing Python is `for i in range(len(xs)): x = xs[i]`. Python's iteration idioms exist to delete that index arithmetic, and each deletion removes a place for an off-by-one to live.

enumerate(xs) yields (index, element) pairs, so when you need BOTH the position and the value — 'return the index of the first duplicate' — you write `for i, x in enumerate(xs)`. The start= parameter (enumerate(xs, start=1)) handles 1-based output requirements without sprinkling i+1 through your code.

zip(a, b) walks two (or more) sequences in lockstep, stopping at the SHORTEST — silently, which is occasionally a bug you should know about (Python 3.10+ adds strict=True to raise on mismatch instead). Three zip idioms carry real interview weight: `dict(zip(keys, values))` builds a lookup table in one expression; `zip(*matrix)` transposes a matrix — the * unpacks the rows as separate arguments, so zip regroups them column-wise; and `zip(xs, xs[1:])` pairs each element with its successor, which is the clean way to ask 'is this sorted?', compute gaps, or find adjacent violations without touching an index.

Unpacking is the third leg. Tuple assignment `a, b = b, a` swaps without a temporary — the right side is built as a tuple before the left side binds, which is also why `curr, prev = curr + prev, curr` works in Fibonacci loops without staging variables. Star-unpacking `first, *middle, last = xs` splits head and tail declaratively. The underscore is the convention for 'this slot is deliberately ignored' (`_, score = pair`), and it tells your reader — or interviewer — that dropping the value is intentional, not an accident. Function-call unpacking (f(*args)) is the same star doing the same job in the other direction: turning one sequence into many arguments.
sections.code:
# enumerate replaces manual index counters
letters = ["a", "b", "c"]
pairs = [(i, ch) for i, ch in enumerate(letters, start=1)]
assert pairs == [(1, "a"), (2, "b"), (3, "c")]

# zip: lockstep walk; dict(zip(...)) builds lookups
names, scores = ["asha", "vik"], [91, 84]
assert dict(zip(names, scores)) == {"asha": 91, "vik": 84}

# zip stops at the shortest sequence -- silently
assert list(zip([1, 2, 3], "ab")) == [(1, "a"), (2, "b")]

# zip(*matrix) transposes rows into columns
m = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
assert list(zip(*m)) == [(1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6)]

# neighbor pairs: zip a sequence with itself shifted by one
xs = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
gaps = [b - a for a, b in zip(xs, xs[1:])]
assert gaps == [-2, 3, -3, 4]
is_sorted = all(a <= b for a, b in zip(xs, xs[1:]))
assert is_sorted is False

# unpacking: swap, star-split, deliberate ignore
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
assert (a, b) == (2, 1)
first, *middle, last = [10, 20, 30, 40]
assert (first, middle, last) == (10, [20, 30], 40)
_, keep = ("drop", "keep")
assert keep == "keep"

# fibonacci step without a temp: RHS tuple builds before LHS binds
prev, curr = 0, 1
for _ in range(5):
    prev, curr = curr, prev + curr
assert curr == 8
print("iteration idioms OK")

sections.title: 6. String Building: join vs +=, and Why the Difference Is Quadratic
sections.content:
Python strings are immutable: no operation ever edits a string in place; every 'modification' builds a new string. That single fact explains the most commonly cited Python performance trap. `s += piece` inside a loop conceptually allocates a fresh string and copies BOTH s and piece into it, every iteration. Summed over n pieces of similar size, the copying is 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n pieces' worth — O(n²) total work to build an O(n) result. (CPython has an in-place resize optimization that often rescues the plain `s += x` loop in practice, but it is an implementation detail that vanishes the moment a second reference to the string exists — the portable answer, and the one to give in an interview, is that repeated concatenation is quadratic.)

The idiom is: accumulate the pieces in a LIST — appending to a list is amortized O(1) — and call `separator.join(pieces)` once at the end. join makes two passes: one to measure the total length, one to copy each piece exactly once into a correctly sized result. Total: O(n). The separator goes BETWEEN elements, so `', '.join(words)` produces clean comma lists with no trailing-separator surgery. Two practical notes: join accepts any iterable of STRINGS — numbers must be converted first (`'-'.join(str(n) for n in nums)`) or you get a TypeError, and `''.join(...)` with an empty separator is the character-assembly idiom for building a string from computed pieces.

Two neighbors of the same idea complete the section. The split/join round trip `' '.join(messy.split())` normalizes any run of whitespace to single spaces — split() with no argument splits on ANY whitespace run and drops empties, which is what makes the trick work. And when you find yourself assembling many formatted fragments, an f-string per piece plus one join is both the fast and the readable version — the pattern the next two sections build on.
sections.code:
words = ["tea", "chai", "filter", "coffee"]

# join: one measuring pass + one copy pass, O(total length)
line = ", ".join(words)
assert line == "tea, chai, filter, coffee"   # separator BETWEEN, no trailing comma

# the idiom: collect pieces in a list, join once
pieces = []
for w in words:
    pieces.append(w.upper())       # list append: amortized O(1)
assert " ".join(pieces) == "TEA CHAI FILTER COFFEE"

# += in a loop builds a new string every pass (quadratic in principle)
s = ""
for w in words:
    s += w
assert s == "teachaifiltercoffee"   # correct result, wrong scaling story

# join needs strings: convert non-strings first
nums = [1, 2, 3]
assert "-".join(str(n) for n in nums) == "1-2-3"
try:
    "-".join(nums)
    type_error = False
except TypeError:
    type_error = True
assert type_error

# split/join round trip: normalize whitespace
messy = "  too   many    spaces "
assert " ".join(messy.split()) == "too many spaces"

# ''.join for character assembly
assert "".join(ch for ch in "a1b2c3" if ch.isalpha()) == "abc"
print("string building OK")

sections.title: 7. heapq Patterns: Priority Queues Without Writing One
sections.content:
A heap is an array-encoded binary tree maintaining one invariant: every parent ≤ its children, so the minimum lives at index 0. Python's heapq module operates on a plain list — there is no Heap class — which surprises people once and then becomes an advantage: your heap is inspectable, serializable, and has zero ceremony. The API worth memorizing: heapify(xs) reorders a list into a heap in O(n) — cheaper than n pushes, and interviewers ask about exactly that; heappush and heappop are O(log n); the top is ALWAYS xs[0], readable for free. Heaps earn their place whenever you repeatedly need 'the smallest (or largest) so far' while items keep arriving: k-largest/k-smallest, merge k sorted lists, Dijkstra's frontier, task schedulers.

heapq is min-only, which spawns the most-asked follow-up: how do you get a max-heap? Store negated values — push -x, negate again on pop. For records, push tuples: (priority, task). Tuples compare field by field, so the heap orders by priority and breaks ties on the next field — and that is also the trap: if priorities tie and the second field is un-comparable (two dicts, two custom objects), the pop raises TypeError. The standard fix is a monotonically increasing counter in the middle: (priority, count, task) — ties fall through to the counter, which never ties, and insertion order wins.

The top-k pattern deserves its own paragraph because it inverts intuition: to track the k LARGEST items, keep a size-k MIN-heap. The heap's root is the k-th largest so far — the gatekeeper; a newcomer either beats the root (heappushpop swaps it in, one O(log k) operation) or is discarded. n items cost O(n log k), versus O(n log n) for full sorting — the difference you cite when the interviewer asks 'why not sort?'. For one-off small queries, heapq.nlargest(k, xs, key=...) and nsmallest wrap the whole pattern, accept a key function, and are the honest answer when k is small and code brevity matters.
sections.code:
import heapq

nums = [7, 2, 9, 4, 1, 8]

# heapify: O(n); the minimum is always at index 0
h = nums[:]
heapq.heapify(h)
assert h[0] == 1
assert heapq.heappop(h) == 1 and h[0] == 2

# max-heap idiom: store negatives
mx = [-n for n in nums]
heapq.heapify(mx)
assert -heapq.heappop(mx) == 9

# top-k largest via size-k MIN-heap: O(n log k)
def k_largest(xs, k):
    h = []
    for x in xs:
        if len(h) < k:
            heapq.heappush(h, x)
        elif x > h[0]:                 # beats the gatekeeper?
            heapq.heappushpop(h, x)    # one combined O(log k) op
    return sorted(h, reverse=True)
assert k_largest(nums, 3) == [9, 8, 7]

# nlargest/nsmallest: the one-liner with key support
words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana"]
assert heapq.nlargest(1, words, key=len) == ["banana"]
assert heapq.nsmallest(2, nums) == [1, 2]

# tuple entries: (priority, count, task) -- counter breaks ties safely
pq = []
for count, (pri, task) in enumerate([(2, "email"), (1, "deploy"), (1, "standup")]):
    heapq.heappush(pq, (pri, count, task))
assert heapq.heappop(pq)[2] == "deploy"     # pri 1, inserted first
assert heapq.heappop(pq)[2] == "standup"    # pri tie -> counter decides
print("heapq idioms OK")

sections.title: 8. bisect Patterns: Binary Search You Don't Have to Debug
sections.content:
Binary search is famously easy to describe and famously easy to get wrong — the off-by-one in the midpoint update has its own literature. The bisect module gives you the two correct primitives pre-debugged, and most interview binary-search tasks reduce to them. Both operate on an already-sorted list in O(log n).

bisect_left(xs, x) returns the FIRST index where x could be inserted while keeping order — for duplicates, the position of the leftmost equal element. bisect_right (alias bisect) returns the position AFTER the last equal element. The pair composes into every classic query on sorted data: bisect_right − bisect_left counts occurrences of x; bisect_left is 'first index ≥ x' (the lower bound of C++ lore); bisect_right is 'first index > x'; and membership is 'bisect_left, then check the element there'. If you internalize one mental model, make it this: bisect answers 'how many elements are strictly less than x' (bisect_left) or '≤ x' (bisect_right) — everything else is arithmetic on those two numbers.

insort(xs, x) inserts while keeping the list sorted — but honestly note its cost when asked: the search is O(log n), the insertion shifts elements, so the operation is O(n). Fine for maintaining a small sorted list under occasional inserts; wrong as the inner loop of a hot path (that is where heaps or balanced-tree libraries come in).

The pattern that impresses: table lookup by boundary. Grading (scores to letters), tax slabs, percentile buckets — any 'which bucket does this value fall into' question is one bisect call against a breakpoints list, replacing an if/elif ladder that grows with every bucket. Since Python 3.10 the bisect functions also accept a key= function, which lets you search lists of records directly. And when the interviewer says 'no library binary search', write the loop but SAY you would normally use bisect — you demonstrate both the algorithm and the judgment.
sections.code:
import bisect

xs = [10, 20, 20, 30]

# bisect_left: leftmost insertion point; bisect_right: past the dupes
assert bisect.bisect_left(xs, 20) == 1
assert bisect.bisect_right(xs, 20) == 3

# occurrences of x in a sorted list, O(log n)
assert bisect.bisect_right(xs, 20) - bisect.bisect_left(xs, 20) == 2

# mental model: '# elements < x' and '# elements <= x'
assert bisect.bisect_left(xs, 25) == 3    # three elements are < 25
assert bisect.bisect_right(xs, 10) == 1   # one element is <= 10

# membership in sorted data without scanning
def contains(sorted_xs, x):
    i = bisect.bisect_left(sorted_xs, x)
    return i < len(sorted_xs) and sorted_xs[i] == x
assert contains(xs, 30) and not contains(xs, 25)

# insort: keeps the list sorted (O(log n) search + O(n) shift)
ys = [1, 3, 5]
bisect.insort(ys, 4)
assert ys == [1, 3, 4, 5]

# boundary-table lookup replaces an if/elif ladder
def grade(score, breakpoints=(60, 70, 80, 90), grades="FDCBA"):
    return grades[bisect.bisect(breakpoints, score)]
assert [grade(s) for s in (55, 60, 75, 90, 99)] == ["F", "D", "C", "A", "A"]
print("bisect idioms OK")

sections.title: 9. Generators and Lazy Evaluation: The Space-Complexity Conversation
sections.content:
A generator is a function that pauses. Where `return` ends a function forever, `yield` hands a value out and FREEZES the function's entire state — locals, loop counters, instruction pointer — until the next value is requested. The consequence: a generator produces values one at a time, on demand, holding O(1) state instead of materializing an O(n) collection. A generator expression `(f(x) for x in xs)` is the same machinery in comprehension clothing — parentheses instead of brackets, nothing computed until something asks.

Why interviews care: space complexity is the second question after time complexity, and generators are frequently the honest answer to 'can you do it in O(1) extra space?' for streaming-shaped problems. `sum(n * n for n in range(10**6))` aggregates a million values while holding one at a time; the listcomp version allocates the entire million-element list first for no benefit. When a genexp is the sole argument to a function, the extra parentheses drop — `sum(x*x for x in xs)` — a small syntax detail that reads as fluency. The built-ins any() and all() add short-circuiting on top of laziness: they stop consuming the moment the answer is decided, so `any(is_prime(n) for n in huge)` may do one predicate call, not millions. Pipelines compose: `sum(1 for line in f if line.strip())` counts non-blank lines while holding one line in memory — the shape of every log-processing answer.

The costs, because honest trade-offs score points: generators are SINGLE-USE (exhausted after one pass — iterating twice silently yields nothing the second time, a real bug class), have no len() and no indexing, and cannot be inspected while debugging without consuming them. Need two passes or random access? Materialize with list(). Generators also model the infinite: itertools.count(1) is an endless stream, safe because islice takes only what you request — the pattern behind 'generate IDs', 'paginate', and lazy test-data factories. The rule to say aloud: generator when the data flows through once; list when you need to hold it.
sections.code:
import itertools

# yield pauses the function and preserves ALL its state
def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1
g = countdown(3)
assert next(g) == 3 and next(g) == 2
assert list(g) == [1]              # resumes where it paused

# genexp: nothing computed until requested -- range(10**9) costs nothing here
gen = (n * n for n in range(10**9))
assert next(gen) == 0 and next(gen) == 1

# aggregation without materializing: one value alive at a time
assert sum(n for n in range(101)) == 5050

# any/all short-circuit: count the predicate calls
def is_even(n):
    is_even.calls += 1
    return n % 2 == 0
is_even.calls = 0
assert any(is_even(n) for n in [1, 3, 4, 9, 11])
assert is_even.calls == 3          # stopped at the first True

# infinite stream + islice: take exactly what you need
naturals = itertools.count(1)
assert list(itertools.islice(naturals, 5)) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# generators are single-use: the second pass is empty
squares = (n * n for n in range(3))
assert list(squares) == [0, 1, 4]
assert list(squares) == []         # exhausted -- a silent bug if unexpected
print("generator idioms OK")

sections.title: 10. Gotchas That Lose Offers: Five Traps and the Object Model Behind Them
sections.content:
Every trap in this section is the same lesson wearing five costumes: Python variables are REFERENCES to objects, and knowing when two references share one object is the whole game. Interviewers use these as calibration questions because each has a surface answer (the rule) and a depth answer (the why).

Mutable default arguments. `def f(x, acc=[])` evaluates the default ONCE, at def time, and stores that single list on the function object. Every call that omits acc gets the SAME list, so state leaks across calls. The idiom: default to None, create inside the body. The why: defaults live in f.__defaults__; the function is an object, created once.

Late-binding closures. `[lambda: i for i in range(3)]` produces three functions that all return 2, because a closure captures the VARIABLE i, not its value at creation — and by call time the loop has finished. Fix: `lambda i=i: i`, which exploits the previous trap deliberately — defaults bind at definition time, freezing the current value.

is versus ==. `==` asks 'equal values?'; `is` asks 'the very same object?'. Use `is` only for singletons — None, True, False — where identity is the actual question. Testing values with `is` appears to work in scary-specific cases: CPython pre-creates the integers -5 through 256, so any reference to 256 is the same cached object while two separately constructed 257s are not. Code that 'worked' with small numbers breaks with big ones — a bug that hides until production.

Shallow copies and the multiplication trap. `[[0]*3]*3` builds ONE inner row and three references to it; writing grid[0][0] changes every 'row'. The fix is a comprehension creating a fresh row per iteration. Same story one level up: copy.copy (and a[:], and dict.copy()) duplicate the outer container while inner objects stay shared; copy.deepcopy recursively duplicates the whole tree. Interviewers reach grid problems fast, so this trap has an outsized hit rate — and explaining it in reference-vocabulary ('three references, one list') is what separates the memorized fix from understanding.
sections.code:
import copy

# 1. mutable default: evaluated once, shared across calls
def bad_append(x, acc=[]):
    acc.append(x)
    return acc
assert bad_append(1) == [1]
assert bad_append(2) == [1, 2]         # same list survived!

def good_append(x, acc=None):
    if acc is None:
        acc = []                       # fresh list per call
    acc.append(x)
    return acc
assert good_append(1) == [1] and good_append(2) == [2]

# 2. late-binding closures capture the variable, not the value
fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
assert [f() for f in fns] == [2, 2, 2]
fixed = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]   # default freezes the value
assert [f() for f in fixed] == [0, 1, 2]

# 3. is vs ==: identity vs equality; 'is' is for None and friends
assert [] == [] and [] is not []
x = None
assert x is None

# 4. shallow copy and the [[0]*3]*3 trap
grid_bug = [[0] * 3] * 3               # three references to ONE row
grid_bug[0][0] = 9
assert grid_bug[1][0] == 9             # every 'row' changed
grid_ok = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]  # fresh row each iteration
grid_ok[0][0] = 9
assert grid_ok[1][0] == 0
nested = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
sh, dp = copy.copy(nested), copy.deepcopy(nested)
nested[0].append(99)
assert sh[0] == [1, 2, 99] and dp[0] == [1, 2]

# 5. small-int caching: why 'is' lies about numbers
a, b = int("256"), int("256")
c, d = int("257"), int("257")
assert a is b                          # -5..256 are pre-created singletons
assert c is not d and c == d           # equal values, distinct objects
print("gotcha demos OK")

sections.title: 11. f-String Fluency: Debugging and Formatting at Typing Speed
sections.content:
In a live interview, every second spent fighting print statements is a second not spent on the algorithm — and messy debug output slows YOU down when you read it. f-strings (formatted string literals, Python 3.6+) put expressions directly inside string braces, evaluated at runtime, and they carry a few tricks that make interview debugging near-free.

The headline trick is the = specifier (3.8+): `f"{x=}"` expands to the literal text of the expression, an equals sign, and its value — `x=10`. It works on arbitrary expressions (`f"{len(queue)=}"` → `len(queue)=3`), which turns the classic three-line labeled print into a one-liner you can sprinkle and delete fast. Pair it with !r, the repr conversion: `f"{s!r}"` prints 'chai' WITH quotes, which is how you notice the trailing whitespace or the string-that-should-be-int that == comparisons hide. When your loop 'looks right' but asserts fail, `f"{i=} {window=} {best=}"` per iteration is the fastest tracer you can type.

After the colon come format specs, the mini-language: `:.2f` fixes decimals (the float-noise suppressor for averages and probabilities); `:,` groups thousands (1,234,567 — instantly readable magnitude); `:.1%` multiplies by 100 and appends % (hit rates, cache ratios); `:03d` zero-pads. Alignment — `:<10` left, `:>10` right, `:^10` center — builds readable tables when you dump a DP matrix or compare expected/actual columns, and the width can itself be a variable via nesting: `f"{name:>{w}}"`. None of this is decoration: a zero-padded, aligned dump of your DP table is often the exact moment you SEE the off-by-one.

One etiquette note: sprinkle f-string debugging freely while solving, narrate what you are checking ('printing the window bounds each step'), and then DELETE the prints before declaring done. Interviewers read leftover debug output as a hygiene signal, the same way reviewers do.
sections.code:
value = 41.99999
name = "latency"

# expressions evaluate inside braces; format spec after the colon
assert f"{name}: {value:.2f}" == "latency: 42.00"

# {expr=} prints the expression AND its value -- the debug one-liner
x = 10
assert f"{x=}" == "x=10"
assert f"{x + 1=}" == "x + 1=11"      # source text is preserved
queue = [1, 2, 3]
assert f"{len(queue)=}" == "len(queue)=3"

# !r shows repr: quotes reveal hidden whitespace and wrong types
s = "chai "
assert f"{s!r}" == "'chai '"          # the trailing space is now visible

# alignment and padding: tables without manual spaces
assert f"{'id':<4}|{'name':>6}" == "id  |  name"
assert f"{7:03d}" == "007"

# thousands separators and percentages
assert f"{1234567:,}" == "1,234,567"
assert f"{0.256:.1%}" == "25.6%"

# nested spec: the width can be a variable
w = 8
assert f"{'hi':>{w}}" == "      hi"

# a DP-row dump that lines up -- where off-by-ones become visible
row = [0, 1, 3, 6]
dump = " ".join(f"{v:>3}" for v in row)
assert dump == "  0   1   3   6"
print("f-string idioms OK")

sections.title: 12. itertools That Impress Honestly: groupby, product, accumulate, chain
sections.content:
itertools is a box of composable iterator algebra, and a handful of its tools map directly onto interview sub-problems. 'Honestly' is in the title because the goal is not sprinkling exotic imports to look clever — it is replacing hand-rolled loops with a named tool WHEN the name says exactly what you mean, and being able to explain the mechanics when asked.

groupby(iterable, key=) collapses CONSECUTIVE runs of equal keys — and that word consecutive is the gotcha interviewers know: on unsorted input, groupby produces one group per run, not per distinct value. For global grouping you either sort by the same key first (O(n log n)) or use the defaultdict(list) pattern from section 1 (O(n), usually the better answer — say so). On the flip side, run-collapsing is exactly what run-length encoding, 'count consecutive repeats', and streak-finding problems want, and there groupby without sorting is the precise tool. Each group is itself a lazy iterator, consumed once — materialize with list(g) if you need it twice.

product(a, b) — or product(xs, repeat=2) — generates the cross product, replacing nested loops with one flat, readable loop header: dice outcomes, coordinate grids, parameter sweeps. combinations(xs, k) yields order-free selections (pairs of teammates), permutations(xs, k) ordered arrangements (podium finishes); both emit tuples lazily, which matters because their counts explode combinatorially — generate-and-filter with these is fine for interview-sized inputs and a stated trade-off for real ones.

accumulate(xs) yields running totals — the prefix-sum array that range-sum problems build manually, in one call (and with func=operator.mul or max it generalizes to running products and running maxima). chain(a, b, c) iterates several sequences as one without concatenating — no copies — and chain.from_iterable flattens one level of nesting. islice you met with generators: slicing semantics for iterators that cannot be indexed. Every one of these earns its import by deleting a loop whose only job was bookkeeping.
sections.code:
from itertools import groupby, product, combinations, permutations, accumulate, chain
import operator

# groupby collapses CONSECUTIVE runs -> run-length encoding
s = "aaabbc"
runs = [(k, len(list(g))) for k, g in groupby(s)]
assert runs == [("a", 3), ("b", 2), ("c", 1)]

# unsorted input -> one group per RUN, not per value (the gotcha)
assert [k for k, _ in groupby("abab")] == ["a", "b", "a", "b"]

# global grouping needs a sort by the same key first
words = ["tea", "ate", "bat", "eat"]
key = lambda w: "".join(sorted(w))
groups = {k: sorted(g) for k, g in groupby(sorted(words, key=key), key=key)}
assert groups["aet"] == ["ate", "eat", "tea"]

# product replaces nested loops
dice = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
assert len(dice) == 36 and (6, 6) in dice

# combinations: order-free; permutations: ordered
assert list(combinations("abc", 2)) == [("a", "b"), ("a", "c"), ("b", "c")]
assert len(list(permutations("abc", 2))) == 6

# accumulate: prefix sums in one call; func= generalizes it
xs = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
assert list(accumulate(xs)) == [3, 4, 8, 9, 14]
assert list(accumulate(xs, operator.mul))[-1] == 60
assert list(accumulate(xs, max)) == [3, 3, 4, 4, 5]

# chain: several sequences as one iterator, zero copying
assert list(chain([1, 2], (3,), "ab")) == [1, 2, 3, "a", "b"]
assert list(chain.from_iterable([[1, 2], [3]])) == [1, 2, 3]
print("itertools OK")

interviewQA.q: When would you use Counter versus defaultdict(int) for counting?
interviewQA.a: Both give you increment-without-existence-checks, so the mechanical difference is small; the choice signals what you are doing with the counts. Counter is the right call when you want counting-specific operations afterward: most_common(k) for top-k answers, counter arithmetic (c1 - c2 gives you 'what is missing', the clean solve for 'can you build this ransom note from these letters'), equality comparison for anagrams, and reading a missing key as 0 without inserting it. defaultdict(int) is the better fit when counting is one part of a larger accumulation you will keep mutating by hand, or when you want the general factory pattern — defaultdict(list) for grouping, defaultdict(set) for deduplicated grouping — and the counts are incidental. One subtlety worth volunteering: reading a missing key from a defaultdict INSERTS the default (the read mutates the dict), while Counter's missing-key read does not insert — a real difference if you later iterate the keys.
followUps: What does Counter('aab') - Counter('ab') return, and how would you use it?
Why can reading d[k] from a defaultdict change len(d)?

interviewQA.q: Why is list.pop(0) a problem in a BFS, and what do you use instead?
interviewQA.a: A Python list is a contiguous array. Removing index 0 forces every remaining element to shift one slot left, so pop(0) is O(n) per call. A BFS dequeues every node once, so building the queue on a list turns an O(V + E) traversal into O(V²) on the queue operations alone — the algorithm is correct, the complexity story is broken, and interviewers specifically look for this because it distinguishes candidates who know their data structure costs from those who pattern-match syntax. The fix is collections.deque, a doubly-linked block structure with O(1) append and popleft: build with deque([start]), consume with popleft(), extend with append(). The same reasoning generalizes: insert(0, x) is O(n) for the same shifting reason, and 'which operations are O(1) on this container' is a question you should be able to answer for list, dict, set, and deque before any interview.
followUps: What is deque doing internally to make both ends O(1)?
When is a plain list still the right queue-ish choice?

interviewQA.q: Explain Python's sort stability and a situation where you would rely on it.
interviewQA.a: Stable means elements that compare equal keep their original relative order after sorting — Timsort, Python's sort, guarantees it. The concrete payoff is multi-key sorting in passes: to order employees by department ascending and salary descending WITHIN department, you can sort by salary descending first, then by department — the second sort preserves the salary order inside each department tie-group. This matters when the two directions cannot be combined in one tuple key: numbers can be negated for descending, but strings cannot, so 'score descending, name ascending' fits one tuple key while 'name descending, score ascending as the secondary' may be cleaner as two passes with reverse=True on the final pass. Stability also protects meaning silently: sorting an already-chronologically-ordered event list by user keeps each user's events in time order, which is often an unstated requirement your code preserves for free — and an unstable sort would corrupt without any test noticing immediately.
followUps: Sort a list of (name, score) by score descending, name ascending, in ONE pass.
What are the time and space costs of Python's sort?

interviewQA.q: Why is building a string with += in a loop considered O(n²), and what is the idiom?
interviewQA.a: Strings are immutable, so s += piece cannot extend s in place — semantically it allocates a new string and copies both s and piece into it. On iteration k the copy costs O(k), and summing 1 + 2 + ... + n gives O(n²) total for n pieces. The idiom is to append pieces to a list (amortized O(1) per append) and call ''.join(pieces) once: join measures the total length in one pass, allocates once, and copies each character exactly once — O(n). Worth volunteering the honest nuance: CPython has a refcount-based optimization that often resizes in place and rescues the naive loop in practice, but it is an implementation detail that disappears when another reference to the string exists, so the portable complexity answer — and the code you should write — is the join idiom. Also mention join's contract: it accepts an iterable of strings only, so numeric pieces need str() first, and the separator lands between elements, eliminating trailing-separator cleanup.
followUps: Why does the same += pattern NOT have this problem with lists?
How would you build a CSV line from a list of ints?

interviewQA.q: What does the mutable default argument trap look like, and why does it happen?
interviewQA.a: def f(x, acc=[]) behaves as if acc is fresh per call, but the default is evaluated exactly once — at def time — and stored on the function object (visible in f.__defaults__). Every call that omits acc receives that one shared list, so appends accumulate across calls: f(1) returns [1], f(2) returns [1, 2]. The root cause is the object model: a function is an object created once when def executes, and its defaults are part of that object, not re-run per call. The idiom is a None sentinel — default to None, create the list inside the body — which moves creation to call time. The same one-time evaluation explains why datetime.now() as a default freezes at import time. And the trap has a constructive twin: binding a default is the standard FIX for late-binding closures (lambda i=i: i), because def-time evaluation is exactly the value-freezing behavior you want there.
followUps: When would a mutable default be used deliberately?
What prints: def f(x, when=None): ... versus def f(x, when=datetime.now())?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between is and ==, and when is `is` the correct choice?
interviewQA.a: == calls __eq__ and asks 'do these have equal values?'; `is` compares object identity — the same object in memory, equivalent to id(a) == id(b). The correct uses of `is` are the singletons: x is None (the PEP 8 rule), x is True / is False when you genuinely mean the exact object, and sentinel objects you created to mean 'no argument given'. The trap that makes this an interview classic: `is` on numbers and strings sometimes returns True for implementation reasons — CPython pre-creates ints -5 through 256 as shared singletons, and interns some strings — so a == comparison mistyped as `is` can pass every small-number test and fail in production with 257. The right instinct is: `is` when identity IS the question (None checks, 'did the caller pass anything', cycle detection via id), == for every value comparison. Bonus depth: None checks use `is` not == because a class can override __eq__ to answer True against None, while identity cannot be faked.
followUps: Why does int('257') is int('257') return False while 257 == 257 is True?
How would you implement a sentinel for 'argument not provided' when None is a valid value?

interviewQA.q: How do you get max-heap behavior from Python's heapq, and what is the tuple-tie trap?
interviewQA.a: heapq implements a min-heap only, so the standard idiom is negation: push -x, and negate again when you pop — the smallest negated value corresponds to the largest original. For records, push tuples like (priority, task): tuples compare field by field, so the heap orders on priority first. The trap is what happens on ties: equal priorities make the comparison fall through to the SECOND field, and if that field is un-comparable — two dicts, two custom objects without __lt__ — heappush raises TypeError at an unpredictable moment (only when a tie actually occurs, so it can pass your tests). The standard fix is a monotonically increasing counter as the middle field: (priority, count, item). The counter never ties, so comparison never reaches the item, and as a bonus you get FIFO order among equal priorities. Also worth knowing: heapify is O(n) — cheaper than n pushes at O(n log n) — and heapq.nlargest/nsmallest with key= are the honest one-liners when you need top-k once rather than a live priority queue.
followUps: Why is heapify O(n) when n pushes are O(n log n)?
Design the heap entry for Dijkstra where nodes are custom objects.

interviewQA.q: bisect_left versus bisect_right: what is the difference and when does it matter?
interviewQA.a: Both binary-search a sorted list for an insertion point in O(log n); they differ only on duplicates. bisect_left returns the index of the FIRST element equal to x (equivalently: the count of elements strictly less than x); bisect_right returns the index PAST the last equal element (the count of elements ≤ x). The difference is the whole answer for several classics: occurrences of x in sorted data is bisect_right − bisect_left; 'first index ≥ x' (lower bound) is bisect_left; 'first index > x' (upper bound) is bisect_right; membership is bisect_left then compare the element at that index. For insertion, the choice decides where equal elements land: insort_left places the new item before existing equals, insort_right after — invisible for ints, meaningful when equal-comparing records carry different payloads and order implies priority. The strongest mental model to state: bisect answers counting questions ('how many are < x / ≤ x') and every other query is arithmetic on those two numbers.
followUps: Using only bisect calls, count how many sorted-list elements fall in [lo, hi].
Why is insort O(n) despite the O(log n) search?

interviewQA.q: When would you return a generator instead of a list, and what are the costs?
interviewQA.a: Return a generator when the data flows through a single pass and materializing it buys nothing: streaming transformations, aggregations (sum, min, any over computed values), reading large files line by line, or producing a potentially unbounded sequence (IDs, pages, retries with backoff). The win is space — O(1) live state instead of O(n) — plus short-circuiting: any/all/next stop consuming the moment the answer is known, so work never done is time saved. In complexity discussions this is frequently the answer to 'reduce the extra space'. The costs to state honestly: generators are single-use (a second iteration silently yields nothing — a genuine bug class when a function's caller loops twice), they have no len() and no indexing, you cannot peek without consuming, and debugging by printing consumes them. If the consumer needs multiple passes, random access, or sorting — sorting requires the whole sequence by definition — return a list. The interview-grade summary: generator when describing a stream, list when you need to HOLD the data.
followUps: Why does sorted() on a generator defeat the memory benefit?
What happens if you call len() on a generator, and how do you count it?

interviewQA.q: Explain the late-binding closure bug with [lambda: i for i in range(3)].
interviewQA.a: All three lambdas return 2. A closure captures the VARIABLE i — a reference to the enclosing scope's binding — not the value i had when the lambda was created. Nothing is looked up until a lambda is CALLED, and by then the loop has finished and i's final value is 2, so every call reads the same post-loop binding. This is late binding, and it bites in real code whenever callbacks are created in loops: button handlers, thread targets, scheduled jobs — every callback acting on the last item. Two idiomatic fixes. The default-argument trick, lambda i=i: i, exploits def-time evaluation of defaults to freeze the current value into each function — the mutable-default trap used FOR you. Or a factory function, def make(i): return lambda: i, where each call creates a new scope with its own i binding. The depth answer interviewers want: this is not a lambda quirk — a def inside a loop behaves identically — it is how Python scoping works: closures share the enclosing binding, and loops do not create a new scope per iteration.
followUps: Why does the same pattern work correctly with a generator expression?
Show the factory-function fix and explain why it works.

interviewQA.q: What is wrong with grid = [[0] * 3] * 3, and what is the reference-model explanation?
interviewQA.a: The inner [0] * 3 creates ONE list object; the outer * 3 then creates a list of three REFERENCES to that single object — not three rows. Writing grid[0][0] = 9 mutates the one shared row, so grid[1][0] and grid[2][0] read 9 too, and a DP or board solution corrupts on the first cell write. The reason the inner multiplication is safe while the outer is not: the inner list contains ints, which are immutable — 'shared' immutable objects cannot be mutated through, so sharing is harmless; the outer list contains a mutable list, where sharing means every alias sees every write. The idiom is a comprehension that evaluates the row expression fresh per iteration: [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]. Verify understanding with identity: all(row is grid[0] for row in grid) is True for the buggy version. The same model explains shallow versus deep copy — copy.copy duplicates the outer container while inner objects stay shared; deepcopy recursively duplicates — and why a[:] copies the list but not the lists inside it.
followUps: When is [x] * n actually the right construction?
How would you deep-copy a 2D grid without importing copy?

interviewQA.q: What does zip do when its inputs have different lengths, and how do you exploit zip idiomatically?
interviewQA.a: zip stops at the shortest input — silently, dropping the tail of longer sequences. That default is occasionally a feature (pairing a sequence with its own shifted self necessarily has unequal lengths) and occasionally a data-loss bug (zipping records with a mismatched column); Python 3.10+ added zip(a, b, strict=True) to raise ValueError on mismatch, and itertools.zip_longest pads with a fillvalue when you want the long tail kept. The idioms worth having ready: dict(zip(keys, values)) builds a mapping in one expression; zip(*matrix) transposes — the star unpacks rows as separate arguments and zip regroups them column-wise; and zip(xs, xs[1:]) yields each adjacent pair, which answers 'is it sorted' (all(a <= b for a, b in ...)), computes deltas, and finds violations without index arithmetic — the shifted copy is one shorter, and zip's stop-at-shortest is exactly the behavior that makes it correct. Note zip returns a lazy iterator: single-use, materialize with list() if you need two passes.
followUps: Why does zip(*m) transpose — walk through the mechanics.
When would zip_longest be the correct choice over strict=True?

interviewQA.q: Name comprehension anti-patterns — when is a comprehension the WRONG choice?
interviewQA.a: Four cases. First, side effects: [print(x) for x in xs] or [out.append(x) for x in xs] build a throwaway list of Nones to smuggle a statement into expression position — a loop states the intent and allocates nothing. Second, early exit: comprehensions cannot break; searching for the first match with a full comprehension does O(n) work where next((x for x in xs if pred(x)), default) or a loop stops immediately — on a 'find first' question that is a complexity difference, not a style one. Third, deep nesting or complex logic: past two for-clauses or with multi-branch conditionals, the one-liner stops being readable in an interview where a stranger must follow your code in real time; unrolling to a loop with named intermediates is the professional move. Fourth, state carried across iterations — running maxima, state machines, accumulators: comprehension elements are independent by design, so threading state through one fights the construct. The positive rule: comprehension when declaring WHAT a collection is; loop when describing HOW a process unfolds.
followUps: Rewrite a triple-nested comprehension you've seen into readable loops.
Is a comprehension faster than the equivalent loop, and why?

interviewQA.q: How would you find the k largest elements, and how does the approach change with k?
interviewQA.a: Three regimes, and naming them is the answer. When k is tiny relative to n, keep a size-k min-heap: the root is the current k-th largest, each new element either beats the root (heappushpop, O(log k)) or is skipped — O(n log k) time, O(k) space, and it works on a stream you cannot hold in memory. In Python: heapq.nlargest(k, xs) wraps this pattern and accepts key=. When k is close to n, sort and slice — sorted(xs, reverse=True)[:k] — O(n log n) but with excellent constants and a single line whose correctness needs no argument; for interview-sized inputs this is often the honest choice, stated with its complexity. When only average-case linear time makes the cut, quickselect partitions to the k-th boundary in expected O(n) — worth describing, rarely worth hand-coding unless asked. The senior moves: ask whether the data is a stream or in memory (streams force the heap), whether you need the k results SORTED (heap contents need a final O(k log k) sort), and say the nlargest one-liner exists before writing the manual heap — writing library-replaceable code without acknowledging it reads as not knowing the library.
followUps: Why is the heap for k-largest a MIN-heap and not a max-heap?
What does quickselect's worst case look like, and how is it mitigated?

interviewQA.q: What is the groupby gotcha, and when is groupby the right tool versus defaultdict?
interviewQA.a: itertools.groupby groups CONSECUTIVE elements with equal keys — it collapses runs, not global categories. On unsorted input, 'abab' yields four groups (a, b, a, b), not two, which surprises anyone expecting SQL's GROUP BY. So for global grouping you must sort by the grouping key first, paying O(n log n), and then groupby adds its O(n) pass. That makes the defaultdict(list) pattern — one O(n) pass appending each item to groups[key] — the usually-better answer for plain categorization, and saying that comparison out loud is worth points. groupby wins precisely when runs ARE the question: run-length encoding, longest streak of equal values, collapsing repeated log lines, splitting a sequence at value changes — there the consecutive semantics is the feature and no sort is needed. Two extra sharp edges: each group is a lazy sub-iterator that is invalidated when you advance to the next group, so materialize with list(g) if needed later; and groupby with a key function requires the SAME key used for sorting, or groups split unexpectedly.
followUps: Write run-length encoding with groupby in two lines.
Why does storing the group iterators for later iteration fail?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between sorted(xs) and xs.sort(), and the classic bug with each?
interviewQA.a: sorted(xs) builds and returns a NEW sorted list and accepts any iterable — generators, tuples, dict keys — leaving the source untouched. xs.sort() sorts the list in place, works only on lists, is slightly cheaper (no copy), and returns None. The classic bug: xs = xs.sort() — Python's convention is that in-place mutators return None so you cannot silently confuse mutation with creation, and this line assigns None to xs, usually exploding later at a distance from the cause. The mirrored bug: calling sorted(xs) and discarding the result, expecting xs to have changed. Both take key= and reverse=, both are stable, both run Timsort at O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space. Choosing between them is a statement of intent worth verbalizing: sort() when the list's order IS the state you are maintaining and no other reference needs the old order; sorted() when the original must survive, when the input is not a list, or in an expression position (sorted(d.items(), key=itemgetter(1)) feeding a loop).
followUps: Why do Python's in-place methods return None by convention?
How do you sort a dict by value and what do you get back?

interviewQA.q: How do you use enumerate and unpacking to avoid index arithmetic, and why do interviewers care?
interviewQA.a: The tell they watch for is for i in range(len(xs)): x = xs[i] — correct, but it reintroduces the index bookkeeping Python's iteration protocol exists to remove, and off-by-ones live in exactly that bookkeeping. The idioms: for x in xs when only values matter; for i, x in enumerate(xs) when the position matters too, with start=1 handling one-based output without i+1 scattered through the body; for a, b in zip(xs, ys) for parallel walks; and for k, v in d.items() instead of indexing d[k] inside a keys loop. Tuple unpacking extends the same principle: a, b = b, a swaps without a temporary (the right side builds a tuple before the left binds — the same guarantee that makes prev, curr = curr, prev + curr correct in a Fibonacci loop); first, *rest = xs splits declaratively; _ marks deliberately ignored slots. Why it matters beyond taste: each idiom deletes a class of bug, and fluent use signals real Python mileage — while genuinely needing the index (in-place writes, two-pointer walks) and using range(len(xs)) THERE is also correct judgment.
followUps: When is range(len(xs)) genuinely the right loop header?
What ordering guarantee makes a, b = b, a safe?

interviewQA.q: Which f-string features actually help during a live coding interview?
interviewQA.a: Three earn their keep. The = specifier: f"{x=}" prints the expression text and its value ('x=10'), and works on arbitrary expressions — f"{len(queue)=}" — so labeled debug output costs one token of typing instead of a sentence; while tracing a sliding window, f"{i=} {window=} {best=}" per iteration is the fastest tracer available. The !r conversion applies repr, printing strings WITH quotes — which is how you spot the trailing space or the '5'-versus-5 type confusion that value printing hides. And format specs for readable output: :.2f to silence float noise, :, for thousands grouping, :>3-style alignment to dump DP rows in columns that line up — misaligned table dumps hide exactly the off-by-one you are hunting. Etiquette completes the answer: narrate what you print ('checking the window bounds each step'), and delete the debug lines before calling the solution done — leftover prints read as hygiene, the same as in code review. All of it is stdlib, zero dependencies, and works in every online judge.
followUps: What does f"{s!r}" show that f"{s}" hides?
How would you dump a 2D DP table so columns align?

flashcards.front: Counter: what do missing keys return, and what is the anagram one-liner?
flashcards.back: Missing keys read as 0 without inserting or raising. Counter(s) == Counter(t) is a complete O(n) anagram check because Counters compare by their counts.

flashcards.front: The grouping idiom with defaultdict
flashcards.back: groups = defaultdict(list); groups[key].append(item) — the first touch of a missing key calls the factory and creates the empty list, so no existence checks.

flashcards.front: defaultdict subtlety: what does READING a missing key do?
flashcards.back: It inserts the default into the dict (the read mutates it, len grows). Counter's missing-key read returns 0 without inserting — a real difference if you iterate keys later.

flashcards.front: Why deque over list for a queue?
flashcards.back: list.pop(0) shifts every remaining element: O(n) per dequeue, turning BFS quadratic. deque gives O(1) append and popleft at both ends. deque(maxlen=k) is a self-evicting last-k window.

flashcards.front: Sort by score descending, name ascending — one pass
flashcards.back: sorted(xs, key=lambda s: (-s[1], s[0])) — negate the numeric field for descending; tuples compare field by field, so ties fall through to the name.

flashcards.front: What does sort stability guarantee and what idiom does it enable?
flashcards.back: Equal-key elements keep their original relative order. Enables multi-pass sorting: sort by the SECONDARY key first, then the primary — the second pass preserves order within ties.

flashcards.front: The xs.sort() return-value bug
flashcards.back: In-place mutators return None by convention, so xs = xs.sort() assigns None. xs.sort() mutates in place; sorted(xs) returns a new list and accepts any iterable.

flashcards.front: itemgetter(1) vs lambda p: p[1]
flashcards.back: Same key behavior; itemgetter is faster and reads as intent for plain field lookups. attrgetter('age') is the object-attribute version. From the operator module.

flashcards.front: Trailing if vs conditional expression in a comprehension
flashcards.back: [f(x) for x in xs if pred(x)] — the trailing if FILTERS elements out. ['a' if pred(x) else 'b' for x in xs] — the conditional expression TRANSFORMS every element. They combine.

flashcards.front: When must a comprehension become a loop? (4 cases)
flashcards.back: Early exit needed (comprehensions can't break); side effects in the body; nesting/logic past easy reading; state carried across iterations (running max, accumulators).

flashcards.front: Find the first matching element lazily, with a default
flashcards.back: next((x for x in xs if pred(x)), None) — the generator stops at the first hit; the second argument is returned if nothing matches (otherwise next raises StopIteration).

flashcards.front: s[a:b:c] — the three rules that prevent off-by-ones
flashcards.back: stop is exclusive; len(s[a:b]) == b - a; omitted parts default to the ends. Negative indices count from the end; negative step walks backward (s[::-1] reverses).

flashcards.front: Do list slices copy or view?
flashcards.back: Always a NEW list: a[:] is the copy idiom, but every slice costs O(k) — recursing on xs[1:] turns linear algorithms quadratic; pass indices instead.

flashcards.front: Slice vs index on out-of-range positions
flashcards.back: Slices clamp silently: s[5:100] stops at the end. Indexing raises IndexError: s[100] blows up. Knowing which forgives is worth an edge case in most string problems.

flashcards.front: Rotate a list right by k, edge-safe
flashcards.back: k %= len(xs), then xs[-k:] + xs[:-k] (guard k == 0, where -0 makes both slices misbehave: return xs[:]). The modulo handles k larger than the length.

flashcards.front: The zip length rule and the fixes
flashcards.back: zip stops at the shortest input, silently. 3.10+: strict=True raises on mismatch. itertools.zip_longest pads with fillvalue. zip(xs, xs[1:]) exploits the rule for neighbor pairs.

flashcards.front: Transpose a matrix in one expression
flashcards.back: list(zip(*m)) — the star unpacks rows as separate arguments; zip regroups them column-wise into tuples. Rows come back as tuples; map to list if mutation is needed.

flashcards.front: Why does a, b = b, a work without a temp?
flashcards.back: The right-hand side is evaluated fully into a tuple BEFORE the left side binds. Same guarantee makes prev, curr = curr, prev + curr correct in Fibonacci loops.

flashcards.front: Why is += string building quadratic, and the fix?
flashcards.back: Strings are immutable: each += copies everything built so far, summing to O(n²). Fix: append pieces to a list, then ''.join(pieces) once — one measuring pass, one copy pass, O(n).

flashcards.front: Two contract details of str.join
flashcards.back: The separator goes BETWEEN elements (no trailing-separator cleanup), and every piece must be a str — '-'.join(str(n) for n in nums) for numbers, else TypeError.

flashcards.front: Normalize messy whitespace in one line
flashcards.back: ' '.join(messy.split()) — split() with no argument splits on any whitespace run and drops empties, so the join rebuilds with single spaces.

flashcards.front: heapq essentials: structure, cost, max-heap
flashcards.back: Operates on a plain list; xs[0] is always the minimum. heapify is O(n); push/pop are O(log n). Max-heap: push negated values, negate on pop.

flashcards.front: Top-k largest: which heap and why?
flashcards.back: A size-k MIN-heap — its root is the k-th largest so far, the gatekeeper. New element beats the root? heappushpop. Total O(n log k) vs O(n log n) for sorting; O(k) space; works on streams.

flashcards.front: The heap tuple-tie trap and its fix
flashcards.back: (priority, item) raises TypeError when priorities tie and items can't compare. Fix: (priority, count, item) with an increasing counter — never ties, gives FIFO among equals.

flashcards.front: bisect_left vs bisect_right in one sentence each
flashcards.back: bisect_left(xs, x): count of elements < x (leftmost position among equals). bisect_right: count of elements <= x (past the last equal). Occurrences = right - left.

flashcards.front: Membership test on a sorted list via bisect
flashcards.back: i = bisect_left(xs, x); found if i < len(xs) and xs[i] == x. O(log n), and the same i is the lower-bound insertion point.

flashcards.front: What does insort really cost?
flashcards.back: O(log n) to find the spot, O(n) to shift elements for insertion. Fine for small or occasionally-updated sorted lists; wrong in a hot loop — that's heap territory.

flashcards.front: Generator vs list — the decision rule
flashcards.back: Generator when data flows through once (streams, aggregation, any/all short-circuits, unbounded sequences): O(1) live state. List when you need len, indexing, sorting, or multiple passes.

flashcards.front: The single-use generator bug
flashcards.back: An exhausted generator yields nothing on a second iteration — silently. Looping twice over the same genexp processes the second loop zero times. Materialize with list() when reuse is needed.

flashcards.front: Mutable default argument: cause and idiom
flashcards.back: Defaults are evaluated ONCE at def time and stored on the function object, so def f(x, acc=[]) shares one list across calls. Idiom: acc=None sentinel, create the list in the body.

flashcards.front: Late-binding closures: symptom and two fixes
flashcards.back: [lambda: i for i in range(3)] — all return 2; closures capture the variable, looked up at call time. Fixes: lambda i=i: i (defaults bind at def time) or a factory function per value.

flashcards.front: Why is [[0]*3]*3 broken and [[0]*3 for _ in range(3)] fine?
flashcards.back: Outer *3 copies REFERENCES to one row, so one write shows in every 'row'. The comprehension evaluates [0]*3 fresh per iteration. Inner *3 is safe because ints are immutable.

flashcards.front: Shallow vs deep copy in one line each
flashcards.back: copy.copy / a[:] / dict.copy(): new outer container, inner objects still shared. copy.deepcopy: recursively duplicates the whole tree. The difference only matters when inners are mutable.

flashcards.front: When is `is` correct, and why does it 'work' on small ints?
flashcards.back: Only for identity questions: x is None, sentinels, True/False. CPython caches ints -5..256 as singletons, so `is` passes on small numbers and fails on 257 — compare values with ==.

flashcards.front: The f-string debug specifier
flashcards.back: f"{expr=}" prints the source text plus the value: f"{len(q)=}" → 'len(q)=3'. With !r for repr (quotes reveal hidden whitespace), it is the fastest labeled tracer you can type.

flashcards.front: groupby's consecutive-runs semantics
flashcards.back: groupby collapses RUNS of equal keys: 'abab' gives four groups. Global grouping needs a sort by the same key first — or use defaultdict(list) in one O(n) pass. Runs ARE the feature for RLE/streaks.

flashcards.front: accumulate and chain in one breath
flashcards.back: accumulate(xs) yields prefix sums ([3,1,4] → [3,4,8]); func=max or operator.mul generalizes to running max/product. chain(a, b) iterates sequences as one, zero copies; chain.from_iterable flattens one level.

flashcards.front: combinations vs permutations vs product
flashcards.back: combinations(xs, k): order-free selections. permutations(xs, k): ordered arrangements. product(a, b) / product(xs, repeat=2): cross product replacing nested loops. All lazy, all emit tuples.
